papers.title: Dysregulation of mechanosensing signaling in monocytes of patients with systemic sclerosis is associated with skin inflammation.
papers.authors: Chaudhary V, Du Y, Mishra B, Ah Kioon MD, Ahuja P, Ivashkiv LB, Truchetet ME, Spiera RF, Lakin K, Gordon JK, Barrat FJ.
papers.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a severe autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by immune dysregulation and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs, resulting in substantial organ dysfunction and increased mortality. Fibrosis is driven in part by infiltration of immune cells, including monocytes that become activated within fibrotic tissue. However, how the mechanical properties of fibrotic skin regulate their function remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that increased stiffness activates human monocytes through mechanosensing. Reanalysis of single cell RNA sequencing datasets revealed that skin infiltrating monocytes exhibit heightened inflammatory signatures as compared to circulating counterparts, with further amplification in SSc. Using collagen-coated hydrogels modeling physiological and fibrotic stiffness, we show that increased stiffness enhances CD86 expression, and broadly upregulates inflammatory transcriptional programs in human monocytes. Mechanistically, stiffness-driven activation was associated with chromatin remodeling and epigenetic reprogramming, identifying the transcription factor Specificity Protein 1 (SP1) as a central regulator. CRISPR-Cas9-mediated disruption or pharmacologic inhibition of SP1 significantly attenuated stiffness- induced inflammatory gene expression, whereas we found no evidence for involvement of the canonical YAP/TAZ-TEAD axis, and pharmacological modulation of PIEZO1 neither reproduced nor blocked the response. Further, monocytes from patients with SSc displayed altered transcriptional trajectories and an exaggerated inflammatory response to high stiffness, accompanied by reduced expression of wound healing and antifibrotic programs. Together, these findings identify SP1-dependent mechanosensing as a previously unrecognized pathway controlling human monocyte activation in the skin and provide mechanistic insight into how tissue stiffness sustains inflammation in SSc.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

papers.title: Correction: Shared immune-inflammatory gene networks and drug prediction in polycystic ovary syndrome and type 2 diabetes mellitus: a bioinformatics and experimental validation study
papers.authors: Liu X, Wang Y, Bi Q, Zhang Y, Wang S, Yang P, Pei J, Zhu W, Chen Y, Zhang Z, Chen B, Zhang Q, Zhang Y, Jiang T.

papers.title: CLEC1B and RAC1 in peripheral immune remodeling associated with sleep disturbance: an exploratory integrative study.
papers.authors: Li Y, Liu C, Zheng H, Lin J.
papers.abstract: Background Sleep disturbance is closely linked to immune dysfunction, but the molecular features of associated peripheral immune remodeling remain incompletely defined. Results In this exploratory study, we integrated blood eQTL data and GWAS summary statistics with mouse PBMC single-cell data, a human PBMC transcriptome cohort, and mouse PBMC measurements. The single-cell dataset comprised one control, one 24-hour sleep-deprivation, and one 48-hour sleep-deprivation library. Descriptive single-cell patterns showed contraction of the B-cell compartment and expansion of granulocytes. Mendelian randomization nominally prioritized RAC1 and CLEC1B, with limited co-localization support. Both genes showed lower expression in the human cohort and were associated with altered B-cell communication and metabolic states. In mouse PBMCs (n = 3 per group), Clec1b qPCR showed a downward trend (P = 0.072), whereas Rac1 qPCR expression was lower after sleep deprivation (P = 0.017). Lane-level western blot analysis also showed lower CLEC1B (P = 0.0056) and RAC1 (P = 0.0016) protein abundance. Conclusions These exploratory integrative analyses nominate CLEC1B and RAC1 as candidate genes associated with peripheral B-cell remodeling in a sleep-disturbance context. These hypothesis-generating findings warrant targeted functional studies of their roles in sleep-related immune remodeling.

papers.title: Synergizing Short-Course Radiotherapy with Immunotherapy in Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: Current Evidence, Challenges, and Future Directions.
papers.authors: Xu L, Jiao Y, Wei Y, Luo M.
papers.abstract: Opinion statement The management of locally advanced rectal cancer is increasingly moving beyond a uniform cytotoxic framework toward biomarker-informed multimodal treatment. Short-course radiotherapy (SCRT) is an established and convenient radiotherapy option and may also provide an immunomodulatory context for immune checkpoint blockade. Preclinical evidence suggests that hypofractionated radiotherapy can promote immunogenic cell death and modulate the tumor immune microenvironment; however, whether the fractionation schedule of SCRT provides a clinically meaningful immunological advantage over long-course chemoradiotherapy remains uncertain. Early randomized studies of SCRT-based chemoimmunotherapy in predominantly proficient mismatch repair/microsatellite-stable (pMMR/MSS) populations have reported encouraging improvements in pathological or overall complete response rates compared with their respective control regimens. Nevertheless, differences in comparator arms, chemotherapy exposure, immunotherapy schedules, endpoint definitions, and follow-up duration preclude firm conclusions regarding the optimal radiotherapy backbone or long-term survival benefit. These findings support further prospective evaluation of SCRT-based combinations and response-adapted non-operative management in appropriately selected patients. Longitudinal circulating tumor DNA, multi-omics profiling, MR-guided adaptive radiotherapy, and computational models such as "digital twins" may contribute to improved patient selection and surveillance, but their clinical utility requires prospective validation.

papers.title: Ontogenically distinct macrophages occupy discrete kidney niches and contribute to monocyte recruitment in experimental crescentic glomerulonephritis.
papers.authors: Chang DY, Sun Z, Li X, Cai W, Zhang W, D'Agati VD, Salant D, He JC, Fu J, Lee K.
papers.abstract: Introduction Crescentic glomerulonephritis (cGN) is characterized by aggressive immune-mediated glomerular injury with prominent macrophage accumulation that correlates with disease severity. However, the distinct contributions of kidney-resident macrophages (KRMs) of different ontogenies remain poorly defined. Methods To explore this, we used single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), reporter-based bone marrow chimeras, timed clodronate liposome treatment, and chemokine blockade to define the spatiotemporal dynamics and functional roles of macrophage populations in nephrotoxic serum nephritis (NTSN), a model of cGN. Results ScRNA-seq of total kidney and CD45 + immune cells revealed that proliferating macrophages and infiltrating monocytes expanded sharply by day five and declined by day ten, indicating that local proliferation, in addition to monocyte recruitment, contributes substantially to early macrophage accumulation in NTSN. Two major KRM subpopulations were distinguished by high Ccr2 or Mrc1 expression, consistent with bone marrow and embryonically seeded, self-renewing KRM population, respectively. In Cx3cr1-GFP recipient mice reconstituted with Ccr2-RFP + donor bone marrow, embryonic-derived GFP + KRMs were enriched in the outer medulla and corticomedullary region, whereas donor-derived RFP + monocytes/macrophages preferentially accumulated in the cortex, including within and around the inflamed glomeruli. A timed clodronate liposome regimen that preferentially reduced recipient-retained GFP + KRMs decreased the cortical accumulation of RFP + cells, albuminuria, and histologic kidney injury in NTSN mice. Cell-cell communication analysis identified macrophage-associated CCL12 expression, a murine ortholog of human CCL2, as a candidate mediator of cortical CCR2 + monocyte recruitment. CCL12 neutralization reduced cortical monocyte accumulation and ameliorated kidney damage in NTSN mice. Conclusion These findings indicate that ontogenically distinct and spatially segregated macrophage populations cooperate during early cGN and support further investigation of the CCR2 axis as a therapeutic target for macrophage-mediated kidney injury in cGN.

papers.title: Blinatumomab in dermatomyositis and refractory ANCA-associated vasculitis: a 2-patient exploratory study.
papers.authors: Lu C, Jin X, Dai J, Shen N, Ma S, Xu X, Li X, Chen L, Jiang G, Ye Q, Zhou Q, Lu L, Han Y.
papers.abstract: Objectives This study aims to explore the safety and efficacy of blinatumomab for the treatment of autoimmune diseases. Methods Two patients, 1 with dermatomyositis (DM) and 1 with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV), were treated with blinatumomab (CD19 × CD3 bispecific T-cell engager antibody) administered by continuous intravenous infusion for 2 cycles. Evaluations were conducted every 2 weeks until week 12, and then once every 4 weeks during continued follow-up through week 24, as well as on week 56. Immune cell dynamics were assessed by flow cytometry and single-cell RNA sequencing. Results During the 14-month follow-up, we observed rapid T-cell activation and B-cell depletion in peripheral blood, together with clinical improvement in both patients, without cytokine release syndrome or other serious adverse events. Moreover, 12 weeks after treatment, both T cells and B cells returned towards a state of homeostasis, accompanied by reduced B-cell activation and downregulation of proinflammatory genes in myeloid compartments. Low-dose blinatumomab treatment was followed by sustained clinical improvement over the 14-month follow-up period, together with marked peripheral B-cell depletion and an acceptable safety and tolerability profile. Conclusions This study provides longitudinal clinical and immunological observations of blinatumomab treatment in anti-Mi-2-positive DM and refractory AAV. These exploratory findings support further evaluation of blinatumomab in autoimmune diseases.

papers.title: Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC.
papers.authors: Xu C, Liu S, Heng Y, Yang C, Cao Y, Gao J, Wei S, Jia D, Liang D, Ma Y, Ng SB, Li H, Zhang X, Gong Y, Shen H, Deng H, Chen A, Xu X, Liao S, Jiang Q, Liu B.
papers.abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies measure multiple molecular layers within intact tissues. Two central challenges are vertical integration, which combines different molecular modalities, and horizontal integration, which aligns cell types across studies. Here we show domain invariant representation through adaptive calibration (DIRAC), a geometric deep learning model that unifies these tasks in a generalized domain adaptation framework. DIRAC learns task-discriminative features that are insensitive to domain shifts caused by batch effects, omic modalities or study sites, enabling a shared embedding space and automated cell-type annotation through label transfer from reference datasets. Across sequencing-based and imaging-based datasets, DIRAC identified a new microvascular proliferation domain in glioblastoma, corrected cortical-layer annotations in severe Alzheimer's disease, resolved subtle structures in mouse embryos and remained robust to missing data and unseen cell types. We generated mouse spleen and thymus Stereo-CITE-seq data and used DIRAC to reveal thymic T cell migration and splenic immune cell interactions. DIRAC is fast and scales to millions of cells.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-driven precision immunogenetics for cancer stem cell-targeted CAR immunotherapy.
papers.authors: Abeysuriya V, Alwis SN, Abeysuriya V.
papers.abstract: Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are a major contributor to therapeutic resistance, tumour recurrence, and disease progression because of their self-renewal capacity, phenotypic plasticity, immune evasion, and ability to persist after treatment. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based immunotherapy has transformed the treatment of several hematological malignancies, but effective targeting of CSC-driven disease, especially solid tumour, remains challenging. Antigen heterogeneity and loss, CSC plasticity, CAR-cell dysfunction, metabolic constraints, and an immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment (TME) can limit long-term therapeutic responses. CSC-associated antigens such as CD133, CD44, EpCAM, HER2, CSPG4, ALDH, and EGFRvIII have been investigated as CAR targets, although their heterogeneous and context-dependent expression raises important concerns regarding CSC specificity and on-target/off-tumour toxicity. Artificial intelligence (AI) and computational approaches provide opportunities to integrate genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, spatial, and clinical data for CSC-associated antigen discovery, biomarker identification, CAR design, patient stratification, and toxicity prediction. However, the evidence supporting these applications varies considerably, ranging from computational and preclinical studies to retrospective clinical modelling, while prospective clinical validation of AI-guided CSC-targeted CAR therapy remains limited. Similarly, next-generation platforms, including CAR-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells, CAR-macrophages (CAR-M), gamma-delta CAR-T cells, and CAR-invariant natural killer T (CAR-iNKT) cells, remain at different stages of translational development. This review critically examines CSC biology, mechanisms of resistance to CAR-based therapy, emerging CAR platforms, and the potential role of AI in precision immunogenetics. Particular emphasis is placed on differentiating CSC-intrinsic, CAR-cell-intrinsic, and TME-mediated resistance and on defining the evidence maturity of AI applications. Finally, current challenges in data availability, tumour heterogeneity, model bias, external validation, interpretability, safety, and prospective clinical translation are discussed, together with priorities for developing clinically validated AI-enabled CSC-targeted CAR therapies.
papers.venue: Journal of the Egyptian National Cancer Institute

papers.title: High Neuronal PAS Domain Protein 2 Expression Associated with Poor Prognosis, Tumor Immune Infiltration, and Adenosine Pathway Markers in Lung Cancer.
papers.authors: Dai J, Reyimu A, Song X, Zhou W.
papers.abstract: This study aims to explore the clinical significance of neuronal PAS domain protein 2 (NPAS2) in lung cancer, its relationship with the tumor immune microenvironment, and its potential upstream non-coding RNA (ncRNA) regulatory network. By analyzing transcriptomic data and clinical information from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database, prognostic genes were identified, and NPAS2 expression was analyzed in lung adenocarcinoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma to determine its associations with patient survival and immune cell infiltration. Immunohistochemical analysis was also performed to compare NPAS2 expression between lung cancer tissues and adjacent non-tumor tissues. NPAS2 expression was elevated in tumor tissues, with higher expression associated with reduced overall survival. This association remained significant in multivariate Cox regression analysis (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.11687, P = 0.0252). In the analyzed dataset, a diagnostic model incorporating NPAS2, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), marker of proliferation Ki-67 (MKI67), and tumor protein p63 (TP63) yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.987. Immune infiltration analysis revealed that in lung adenocarcinoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma, NPAS2 expression was positively correlated with CD4⁺ T cell and neutrophil infiltration, as well as with the expression of the immune checkpoint molecule sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-like lectin 15 (SIGLEC15). Additionally, NPAS2 expression was positively correlated with the adenosine pathway markers CD39 and CD73. Bioinformatics analysis further identified a potential regulatory axis of NORAD/AC087477.2-hsa-miR-106a-5p/hsa-miR-17-5p-NPAS2. These results suggest that NPAS2 may be a candidate biomarker for lung cancer diagnosis and prognosis assessment and may be associated with tumor immune cell infiltration and adenosine-related immune regulatory processes. However, further functional experiments and clinical validation are needed to clarify its potential molecular mechanism and clinical application value.

papers.title: A CD44-regulating Multimodal Therapeutic Strategy for MAFLD-Associated Pancreatic Cancer Liver Metastasis.
papers.authors: Fu S, Shan S, Shi X, Wang W, Wang H, Guo S, Zhao C, Zhang T, Wang F, Castro A, Miranda P, Pardo H, Mombrú D, Romero M, Mombrú AW, Saluja AK, Liu X, Yu Q, Gao C, Ren H.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) has emerged as a novel risk factor for pancreatic cancer, particularly early liver metastasis. However, the underlying mechanisms and effective therapeutic strategies remain largely unclear. Here, based on clinical databases, patient tissue samples, and single-cell sequencing of mouse models, we identified CD44 as a key contributor to MAFLD-associated pancreatic cancer progression. High CD44 expression was significantly associated with poor survival in patients with pancreatic cancer and was further elevated in MAFLD-associated liver metastatic lesions. Considering that the limited effects of single treatment, we developed a cationic DOTAP/cholesterol liposomal nanoplatform co-loaded with gemcitabine, IR780, and CD44 siRNA (GIR@Lip) for combined chemotherapy, photothermal therapy, and immunotherapy. GIR@Lip nanoparticles exhibited excellent size uniformity, stability, and photothermal conversion efficiency, which could efficiently inhibit KPC cells' viability, migration and invasion, downregulate CD44 expression and stimulate immune response. Furthermore, GIR@Lip efficiently accumulated in tumor tissues in vivo, exhibiting a significant reduction in liver metastatic lesions and remodeling the M1 type tumor associated macrophages (TAMs), CD4 + and CD8 + T cells. Collectively, these findings identify CD44 as a potential therapeutic target for MAFLD-associated pancreatic cancer liver metastasis and highlight GIR@Lip as a promising multimodal strategy for its treatment.

papers.title: Hypoxia orchestrates the natural history of inflammatory bowel disease: Mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
papers.authors: Luque MVS, Moreno ASA, Angarita-Planchez ME, Múnera-Rodríguez AM, López-Enríquez S, Casado-Jurado D, de Miguel M, Palomares F.
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) arises from a dynamic interplay between epithelial dysfunction, immune activation, microbial dysbiosis and tissue remodelling. Although hypoxia was initially regarded as a consequence of intestinal inflammation, it is now recognized as an active regulator of epithelial, immune and stromal responses that coordinate disease progression. Here, we propose that hypoxia acts as a biological organizer linking oxygen sensing to the transition from intestinal homeostasis to chronic inflammation and structural tissue damage. We use this term in a mechanistic rather than a hierarchical sense: oxygen availability is a shared upstream constraint on epithelial, immune, microbial and stromal programmes, not a single initiating event. This review integrates evidence connecting oxygen sensing with epithelial barrier integrity, immunometabolism, microbial ecology and stromal remodelling, with emphasis on advances in single-cell transcriptomics, spatial biology and microbiome research. Physiological low-oxygen gradients support epithelial metabolism, barrier integrity and immune tolerance, whereas persistent inflammatory hypoxia drives oxidative stress, metabolic reprogramming and maladaptive epithelial-immune-microbial interactions. Hypoxia also contributes to spatially distinct epithelial, immune and stromal niches that may sustain chronic inflammation and fibrotic progression. Microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids and succinate, together with iron metabolism and ferroptosis, further link oxygen sensing to tissue injury, adaptation and repair. These findings position hypoxia-responsive signalling as a pharmacologically actionable network rather than a downstream consequence of inflammation. Targeting selected components may promote mucosal healing and limit structural disease progression, although successful translation will require cell- and isoform-selective modulation, adequate tissue exposure and careful assessment of long-term safety.

papers.title: The atherosclerotic plaque microenvironment: cellular plasticity, extracellular matrix remodeling, and plaque stability.
papers.authors: Faa G, Piludu M, Piras M, Faa A, Sanfilippo R, Suri JS, Cau R, Saba L.
papers.abstract: The plaque microenvironment (PME) integrates systemic lipid exposure with local vascular, immune and stromal responses. Vascular smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells, monocytes, macrophages, fibroblast-like cells and lymphocytes interact within a continuously remodeled extracellular matrix. Their context-dependent states influence inflammation, lipid handling, matrix organization and the balance between plaque stability and vulnerability. This narrative review examines these cellular and extracellular components, with particular attention to phenotypic modulation, endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition and the limitations of inferring cellular origin from shared markers. Human single-cell findings expand the conventional M1/M2 view of macrophages. Therapeutic evidence is considered across experimental models, human pathology, intravascular imaging and randomized clinical outcome trials. Systemic lipid lowering and selected anti-inflammatory interventions can modify atherosclerotic disease, but changes in plaque composition do not by themselves establish reductions in myocardial infarction or stroke. Carotid and coronary findings also require site-specific interpretation. Integrating mechanistic observations with the level and anatomical setting of the evidence provides a framework for evaluating established therapies and developing selective PME-directed strategies.

papers.title: Model systems and integration strategies to capture human biology.
papers.authors: Chörsi MS, Sayed IM, Jones SN, Bao Z, Wu JC.
papers.abstract: Modelling human biology is difficult precisely because many of the responses that matter most emerge not within a single tissue or cell type, but at the boundaries where matrix, immune and systemic signals converge in ways that are hard to recreate in isolation. Conventional in vitro systems and animal studies have advanced our understanding of many physiological processes, but they still consistently fall short at these interfaces. In this Review, we discuss how engineered materials, organoids, microphysiological systems and computational models can be used together to build more informative human model systems. We first consider engineered materials as tools for controlling the local environment around cells, including matrix composition, stiffness, geometry, transport and time-dependent cues. We then examine organoids, assembloids and microphysiological system platforms, with emphasis on functional benchmarking, vascularization, immune integration, maturation, reproducibility and biological variation across donors and conditions. Finally, we discuss computational models, including spatial atlases, generative models and digital twins, as tools for organizing measurements, testing mechanisms and improving prediction. A key insight is that no current platform fully closes the loop between sensing, tissue modelling, computational calibration and feedback-guided intervention. The central challenge now is to build models whose complexity is justified by the human question they are designed to answer.

papers.title: ExNCDIA: an explainable ensemble learning framework for predicting non-chemotherapy drug-induced agranulocytosis and interpreting structural associations.
papers.authors: Huang X, Jiang S, Liu P.
papers.abstract: Non-chemotherapy drug-induced agranulocytosis (NCDIA) is a rare but life-threatening idiosyncratic toxicity whose mechanisms remain largely unresolved; for a subset of drugs, however, the risk has been linked to chemical structure through bioactivation, whereby reactive intermediates injure neutrophils and myeloid progenitors, and haptenate proteins to trigger immune-mediated destruction. Yet the structural features underlying this liability remain poorly defined, and interpretable models for flagging it during design are scarce. Here we report ExNCDIA, an explainable machine learning framework that predicts NCDIA liability directly from chemical structure. From a curated set of 906 drugs (371 NCDIA-positive and 535 NCDIA-negative), we benchmarked complementary open-source representations and imbalance-aware ensemble classifiers, and retained two balanced random forest models-one trained on RDKit molecular descriptors refined by genetic-algorithm feature selection (test ROC-AUC 0.850, MCC 0.591), the other on MACCS substructure keys (test ROC-AUC 0.847, MCC 0.518). Both showed balanced discrimination in training-set cross-validation and on the held-out test set. Crucially, Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) applied to these two non-overlapping representations converged on the same medicinal-chemistry signal: NCDIA risk rises with sulfur-containing pharmacophores, multiple aromatic rings, and nitrogen-bearing/arylamine cores-motifs prone to cytochrome P450- and myeloperoxidase-mediated oxidation to reactive metabolites-and falls with aliphatic, saturated-oxygenated scaffolds lacking such bioactivatable groups. Delivered as a freely accessible web tool, ExNCDIA couples quantitative prediction with interpretable structural associations, supporting early candidate prioritization and post-marketing risk assessment.

papers.title: Transcriptomic Identification of Candidate Biomarkers Associated With Vascular Calcification-Related Signaling Pathways in Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy.
papers.authors: Cheng L, Xin Z, Zhao X, Wang J.
papers.abstract: Background Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) is one of the most prevalent primary glomerular diseases globally. This study is aimed at identifying candidate biomarkers associated with vascular calcification-related signaling pathways in IgAN and at investigating their potential biological associations. Methods This was an observational bioinformatics study based on public transcriptomic datasets. Vascular calcification-related genes (VCRGs) were defined based on selected KEGG signaling pathways. Data were obtained from public databases. Candidate biomarkers were identified via differential analysis, machine learning, and cross-compartment external expression assessment. Enrichment analysis, immune infiltration, regulatory networks, computational drug prediction, and computational N6-methyladenosine (m6A) site prediction were used to explore the potential biological context of the candidate biomarkers. Results Differential analysis identified 348 differentially expressed genes (DEGs). By intersecting these DEGs with VCRGs, 30 candidate genes were obtained. JUN , FOS , and COL1A2 were finally identified as candidate biomarkers, and these genes were mainly associated with the "Nagashima EGF signaling" and "Nagashima NRG1 signaling." Six differential immune cell types (e.g., M2 macrophages) differed significantly between the IgAN and control groups. Spearman analysis showed that COL1A2 was negatively correlated with resting natural killer (NK) cells (cor = -0.57, p p Conclusion JUN , FOS , and COL1A2 were identified as IgAN-associated candidate biomarkers linked to vascular calcification-related signaling pathway genes, providing exploratory biological insights into the potential molecular links between IgAN and calcification-related signaling.

papers.title: Longitudinal single-cell profiling of breast tumors highlights immune and epigenetic mechanisms associated with sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors.
papers.authors: Altinönder I, Winton V, Quý KL, Fongaard M, Bjørnstad PM, Agustsdottir EES, Geisler SB, Seyedzadeh M, Buvarp UC, Lyngra M, Frigessi A, Lambrechts D, Kristensen V, Mathelier A, Greiff V, Geisler J, Tekpli X.
papers.abstract: Estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer treatment is based primarily on endocrine therapy. To dissect mechanisms of sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors in ER-positive breast cancer, we profiled tumor biopsies from 25 patients during neoadjuvant therapy using single-cell RNA sequencing, immune receptor sequencing and enhancer activity mapping. Malignant cells with high ER signaling and elevated activity of enhancers with ER binding sites were sensitive to treatment. Resistance was associated with androgen receptor signaling, dedifferentiation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Poor responders preferentially used the androgen receptor cis-regulome under treatment pressure. The baseline tumor microenvironment was associated with tumor downstaging. Poor responders exhibited a 'hot', yet ineffective immune landscape enriched for naive lymphoid and undifferentiated myeloid cells. Good responders showed an active immune microenvironment with sustained clonal expansion of T cells. Our longitudinal single-cell analyses elucidate the genetic, cellular and epigenetic mechanisms driving sensitivity and resistance to neoadjuvant aromatase inhibition in ER-positive breast cancer.

papers.title: Cancer patient outcomes correlate with activating-KIR/ligand repertoires associated with distinct NK cell transcriptomic profiles.
papers.authors: Ruiz-Lorente I, Vallejo-Pulido A, López-Abad A, López Cubillana P, Barozi V, Khakoo SI, Minguela A, Gimeno L.
papers.abstract: Background Rates of cancer cure increase; however, recurrence and refractoriness remain clinical challenges that require alternative therapeutic strategies. Natural killer (NK) cells could play a decisive role if their antitumor reactivity can be enhanced. The interaction between killer-cell immunoglobulin-like receptors (KIRs) and their human leukocyte antigen class-I (HLA-I) ligands significantly influences NK-cell education and may impact clinical outcomes in cancer patients. In this study, we evaluated the impact of KIR/HLA-I interactions on the transcriptomic profile of circulating NK-cells and their association with patient outcome. Methods KIR and HLA-I genotyping, together with KIR expression analysis in circulating NK cells, were performed in patients with solid and hematologic malignancies ( n = 1,153). In addition, single-cell transcriptomic analyses (scRNA-seq) of circulating NK and T lymphocytes were carried out in selected donors with KIR/HLA-I genotypes associated with short and long survival. Results Activating KIRs (aKIRs), more than inhibitory KIRs, were associated with cancer patient outcomes. The accumulation of aKIR-HLA interactions was related to shorter overall survival, whereas KIR2DS1/C2 interaction, in the absence of other aKIR interactions, was associated with longer survival. Three major NK-cell transcriptional profiles were identified: mature cytotoxic, immature/regulatory, and adaptive cytotoxic. The adaptive-like transcriptional profile was associated with longer survival. Conclusions In conclusion, aKIR/HLA-I interactions were associated with cancer patient outcomes. In particular, KIR2DS1/C2 interaction in the absence of other activating signals was associated with adaptive NK-cell transcriptomic profiles and improved survival. Understanding the mechanisms underlying effective NK-cell-mediated tumor immunity may provide new opportunities for patients with refractory tumors.

papers.title: The preference of T cell receptor β repertoire in laryngeal cancer.
papers.authors: Pang W, Zhang Z, Kang E, Guo Y, Liang D, Qin Z, Qiu J, Wang H, Wang K, Liang Q.
papers.abstract: Laryngeal cancer (LC), characterized by rapid local infiltration, poor prognosis, and low survival rate, is a common malignant tumor within the head and neck region. Currently, treatment outcomes for LC remain unsatisfactory, including those involving tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy, which has demonstrated effectiveness in solid tumors. The identification of specific T cell receptor (TCR) within TILs in LC may provide novel perspectives for overcoming these therapeutic challenges. In this study, we collected tumor tissues and peritumor tissues from LC patients and used immunohistochemistry to evaluate the infiltration of immune cells. The results revealed that the counts of CD3 + , CD4 + , and CD8 + T cells were considerably enhanced in the LC compared to the peritumor group. Besides, the levels of these infiltrating immune cells exhibited a major positive correlation with serum concentrations of squamous cell carcinoma antigen (SCCA) in LC patients. Moreover, the differences in the usage of TRBV/J segments and complementarity-determining region 3 (CDR3) amino acid motifs were observed between LC and peritumor tissues by using immune repertoire sequencing (IR-Seq) to identify specific TCRs. This study delineates the specific TCR repertoires of TILs in LC patients, emphasizing their potential as candidate repertoire signatures warranting further validation for diagnosis and treatment.

papers.title: Integrated single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analysis suggest a possible association between M1-like macrophage cuproptosis and angiogenic impairment in exercise-deficiency-associated sarcopenia.
papers.authors: Li S, Wu X, Jia R, Liu J, Jia C, Deng L, Xue Q, Li X, Cong F, Wang S, Wei Y, Wang J.
papers.abstract: Sarcopenia is a geriatric syndrome characterized by the progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass and function. While physical inactivity is a primary risk factor of sarcopenia, the underlying molecular mediators remain poorly studied. By combined analysis of human bulk transcriptomic data and single-cell RNA sequencing data, we identified a cuproptosis-associated transcriptional signature significantly enriched in both human sarcopenia and exercise-deprivation models. Our analyses suggest that M1-like macrophage may be particularly vulnerable to cuproptosis due to elevated SLC31A2 expression, potentially contributing to their depletion in the sedentary muscle microenvironment. Intercellular communication modeling further implied that the reduction in M1-like macrophage may impair CXCL8-mediated (or its murine functional analogs) signaling to endothelial tip cells, a process essential for microvascular maintenance. To provide physiological context, we validated these findings in an aged sarcopenia murine model (24-month-old C57BL/6 J). In the gastrocnemius muscle of sarcopenic mice, we observed a significant decrease in muscle fiber cross-sectional area (CSA) alongside a concurrent reduction in F4/80⁺CD86⁺ M1-like macrophage and VEGFR2⁺/CD31⁺ endothelial tip cells. Collectively, our study provides associative link for a candidate mechanistic axis-SLC31A2-mediated cuproptosis in M1-like macrophage-that potentially links physical inactivity to vascular rarefaction in sarcopenia. These findings offer a new framework for investigating the immune-vascular crosstalk in muscle aging and highlight potential therapeutic targets for intervention.

papers.title: A single-cell atlas of pediatric undifferentiated recurrent fever reveals candidate immune regulators.
papers.authors: Jung S, Wiedemuth R, Martinez Perez A, Wannige CT, Strauss T, Körholz J, Pietzsch L, Thieme S, Morbach H, Schuetz C, Del Sol A.
papers.abstract: Children with periodic fever syndromes not attributable to infections, rheumatic disorders, malignancies, or known monogenic autoinflammatory conditions are classified as "syndrome of undifferentiated recurrent fever" (SURF). To date, treatment remains empirical, often resulting in only a partial response, underscoring the unmet clinical need for new therapeutic strategies. To advance the molecular understanding of SURF, we generated a large-scale single-cell RNA-seq immune atlas of 29 SURF patients with more than 200,000 cells. Comparison of patients with three healthy cohorts revealed large-scale metabolic shifts together with a distinct cytokine signature already observable during afebrile periods. This indicates that afebrile SURF cannot be considered a less inflammatory resting state but rather as a distinct homeostatic state. Furthermore, our analysis suggests an NAMPT-mediated autocrine feedback loop connecting the metabolic dysregulations with the pro-inflammatory phenotype in monocytes. This study offers insights into the SURF immunopathology and generates testable hypotheses to guide future therapies.

papers.title: Multi-omics integration identifies core genes, molecular subtypes, and IDI1-centered immune microenvironment mechanisms in coronary artery disease.
papers.authors: Sun Q, Zhou Z, Liang S, Yang H, Wu A.
papers.abstract: Background Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of death worldwide, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Methods We integrated transcriptomic datasets (GSE113079, GSE98583, GSE71226) and single-cell RNA sequencing data (GSE159677) from GEO. Differential expression analysis, WGCNA, machine learning, molecular clustering, immune infiltration analysis, CellChat, in silico knockout, and PheWAS were applied to investigate CAD-related molecular networks. Results We identified 99 DEGs and the MEturquoise module as a CAD-associated module. Machine learning initially identified four candidate genes (RC3H1, IDI1, RAB2A, and SIRPB2); however, only IDI1 was retained after external validation and single-cell intersection. Single-cell analysis revealed macrophage expansion and specific IDI1 enrichment in Cycling cells and immune populations. CAD was classified into two molecular subtypes with distinct immune profiles. Cell communication analysis identified SPP1, TNF, CCL, and MIF pathways as key inflammatory regulators. Virtual knockout simulation of IDI1 affected hemostasis, Toll-like receptor signaling, and collagen degradation pathways. PheWAS showed no significant phenotype-wide associations for IDI1. Conclusion This study identified IDI1 as a CAD-associated candidate gene, revealed immune-based molecular subtypes of CAD, and suggested that IDI1 and inflammatory signaling pathways may serve as potential therapeutic targets, providing insights into precision classification and targeted therapy for CAD.

papers.title: Synthesizing multi-omics evidence of interface-specific selection in lung adenocarcinoma metastasis: A trait-origin-interface-function framework across lymph-node and brain ecosystems.
papers.authors: Xu Y, Zhang R, Hu Y, Yang M, Shan H, Liang T, Guo L.
papers.abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) mortality is driven largely by metastatic progression, yet lymph-node metastasis (LNM) and parenchymal brain metastasis (BrM) arise in fundamentally different immune and anatomical ecosystems. Here, we present an integrative review that conceptually synthesizes published genomic, single-cell, spatial-transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic findings. Our trait-origin-interface-function (TOIF) framework maps individual claims to trait origin, anatomical interface, metastatic stage and functional output, with separate annotations for evidence type and study context. In LNM, lymphatic access and nodal occupation are associated with remodeling of antigen presentation, progenitor T-cell maintenance, lymphoid organization, and immune-cell export; however, evidence for individual tumor-immune communication axes remains uneven. In BrM, neurovascular entry, perivascular survival, glial-myeloid signaling, metabolic adaptation, and restricted effector access represent separable bottlenecks. Cross-platform evidence indicates that shared genomic ancestry can coexist with site-enriched transcriptional, immune, and metabolic states, while temporal and lineage-resolved measurements help distinguish their possible pre-existence, selective expansion and acquisition after tissue exposure. We therefore propose a TOIF framework that links each candidate mechanism to the omics layers that support it, the spatial context in which it operates, and the experiment needed to test causality. This framework clarifies why similar low-cytotoxicity phenotypes may reflect distinct mechanisms in nodal and brain lesions, and provides a basis for multi-omics biomarker development and stage-matched therapeutic investigation in LUAD metastasis.

papers.title: T-cell immunity in anti-tumor battle.
papers.authors: Qin Y, Yan K, Li D, Zhang J, Guo Z, Zhang Y, Lu W.
papers.abstract: The clinical success of T-cell-based immunotherapies has transformed oncology, yet tumor immune evasion remains a formidable barrier. In this review, we delineate the developmental and molecular landscapes that shape antitumor T-cell immunity. Following a brief overview of CD4 + helper T-cell contributions, we focus primarily on CD8 + cytotoxic lineages. Rather than a passive loss of effector function, CD8 + T-cell exhaustion is increasingly recognized as functional attrition and profound oligoclonality. In the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), unremitting antigenic pressure drives an iterative selection process that` narrows a highly diverse T-cell pool into a constricted, oligoclonal population, a phenomenon termed "clonal contraction". We expand the conceptual scale of T-cell clonal selection during the immune response, tracing this clonal evolution from early thymic selection and primary antigen priming to exhaustive terminal differentiation. We further propose a structural model demonstrating how the biophysical constraints of a fixed T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire create a profound imbalance against rapidly diversifying tumor antigens. Within this framework, we highlight tissue-resident memory (Trm) as a crucial spatial reservoir that safeguards the host against the depletion of functional clones. Finally, we contextualize the therapeutic paradigm of immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) and note that, under some circumstances, durable clinical efficacy can be driven by systemic "clonal replacement". Ultimately, we argue that next-generation T-cell-based immunotherapies may shift `from attempting only to reverse functional exhaustion to actively engineering continuous clonal selection and preserving TCR repertoire diversity.

papers.title: Longitudinal remodeling of the tumor-immune microenvironment during regorafenib, nivolumab, and chemotherapy in advanced gastric cancer.
papers.authors: Itahashi K, Kawazoe A, Hashimoto T, Yan Y, Irie T, Ono H, Tamura H, Hongo K, Ikeno T, Wakabayashi M, Sato A, Nakamura Y, Fujisawa T, Iwasawa T, Suzuki T, Nakayama I, Kojima Y, Yoshino T, Nishikawa H, Koyama S, Shitara K.
papers.abstract: Previous studies combining the multikinase inhibitor regorafenib with a PD-1 inhibitor showed promising activity in gastric cancer. We conducted a phase 1b/2 trial (NCT05394740) of first-line regorafenib, nivolumab, and chemotherapy in 30 patients with mismatch repair-proficient gastric cancer and investigated its impact on the tumor microenvironment. The primary end point was met; 22 of 30 patients showed objective tumor response (73%; 80% confidence interval, 60.3 to 83.8). Single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing were performed on biopsy samples at baseline, during treatment, and at disease progression. The combination treatment increased tumor antigen-reactive CD8 + T cells and M1-like proinflammatory macrophages and decreased immunosuppressive and tumor-promoting populations, including activated CCR8 + regulatory T cells, LRRC15 + cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), RGS5 + pericytes, and APLN + tip cells. At progression, LRRC15 + CAFs and APLN + tip cells remained reduced, activated CCR8 + regulatory T cells reexpanded, and additional treatment-resistant subsets emerged, including APOC1 + lipid-associated macrophages. In murine models of acquired resistance, therapeutic targeting of these suppressive immune cell populations with antibodies against CCR8 or TREM2 in combination with PD-1 blockade restored antitumor immunity. These findings demonstrate dynamic remodeling of the tumor microenvironment and suggest potential therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Cancer-specific T cell receptor discovery using 150,000 clinical genomics samples.
papers.authors: Jackson EK, Luo F, Dietze J, Yee C, Martin A, Tatang D, Palowitch GM, Miller H, Manandhar D, Hao Y, Esaulova E, Dulberger C, Roscoe BP, Massaro M, Ward NM, Nicholson T, Funsten M, Gnoth S, Newrzela S, LaHaye S, Vyasamneni R, Srouji JR, Xie YJ, Mikhaylov V, Gaynor RB, Juneja VR, Fields P, Rooney MS.
papers.abstract: T cell receptors (TCRs) can enable detection and elimination of cancer cells via recognition of cancer-specific peptides presented on human leukocyte antigen (HLA). We speculated that shared cancer antigens could be recognized by recurrent ("public") TCRs, which might be identifiable using statistical methods. Here, we identified public TCRs against therapeutically relevant targets via computational analysis of large-scale bulk RNA sequencing data obtained from routine clinical genomics testing. Using data from ∼150,000 patient tumor samples, we identified TCR chains that were associated with well-known cancer antigens, including human papillomavirus, mutated KRAS, and CT83. We devised methods for pairing enriched TCR-α and TCR-β chain sequences and validated 44 TCRs across nine peptide-HLA targets for antigen recognition, including potent cytotoxic TCRs. Our results suggest that public anticancer TCRs are common and may represent a new source for the development of cancer therapeutics.

papers.title: Pulsed Low-dose-rate Radiotherapy Remodels the Tumor Immune Microenvironment and is Associated With Crosstalk Between SPP1⁺ tumor-associated macrophages and GZMK⁺ CD8⁺ T cells.
papers.authors: Zhou Z, Hong Y, You J, Que K, Lan Y, Lin Y, Peng J, Lin Z, Li L, Han L, Xu B.
papers.abstract: Pulsed low-dose-rate radiotherapy (PLDR) is a promising reirradiation strategy for refractory solid tumors because of its potential to reduce normal tissue toxicity; however, its immunomodulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we retrospectively analyzed clinical outcomes and treatment-related adverse events in 16 patients with refractory solid tumors treated with PLDR. Using MC38 tumor-bearing mice, we compared PLDR and conventional radiotherapy (cRT) under biologically equivalent dose conditions and performed single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize treatment-associated remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIM). Multiplex immunofluorescence staining and spatial analysis were further conducted in an independent cohort of 114 patients with rectal cancer to evaluate the clinical relevance of identified immune features. PLDR achieved comparable local tumor control to cRT while reducing treatment-related toxicity and improving overall survival (OS) in mouse models. In the combination-treatment setting, single-cell analyses showed that PLDR + immunotherapy with an anti-PD-1 antibody combined with the targeted agent anlotinib (ITT), compared with cRT + ITT, was associated with enrichment of Gzmk⁺ CD8⁺ T cells, reduced Spp1⁺ tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) abundance, and altered cell-cell communication between these populations. In our independent rectal cancer cohort, the spatial distance between SPP1⁺ TAMs and GZMK⁺ CD8⁺ T cells was independently associated with OS. These findings suggest that the interaction between SPP1⁺ TAMs and GZMK⁺ CD8⁺ T cells may be closely associated with PLDR-related TIM remodeling and may also serve as a potential prognostic biomarker in rectal cancer.

papers.title: Single-cell and spatial characterization of the human pancreas in cystic fibrosis.
papers.authors: Mummey HM, Corban S, Lucero J, Melton RL, Pittigher M, Johnston VC, Deutsch GH, D'Antonio-Chronowska A, Wang A, Hull-Meichle RL, Gaulton KJ.
papers.abstract: Cystic fibrosis (CF) causes severely damaged pancreatic morphology and cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD), but the cellular drivers of CFRD in the pancreas are not understood. Here, we perform single-cell and spatial profiling of 2.04 M cells from 23 non-disease or CF pancreas donors. A high-mucin ductal sub-type had relatively preserved abundance and genomic profiles but altered localization in CF. Changes in inflammatory and fibrotic pathways were driven by crosstalk between immune and pro-fibrotic cells in specific niches. Beta cells had extensive changes in CF, including increased stress responses and evidence for compensatory secretion, that were distinct from those in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Islets localized near large adipose tissue and collagen in CF had reduced beta cells linked to signaling from adipocytes, macrophages, stellate cells, and high-mucin ductal cells. Overall, our results highlight pancreatic microenvironments of beta cell dysfunction in CF and offer in-roads to preserving beta cells in CFRD.

papers.title: Integrative transcriptomic and single-cell analysis identifies a manganese-associated transcriptional signature and a potential JUN/HBEGF-associated endothelial signature in COPD pulmonary vascular remodeling.
papers.authors: Liu Z, Nie L, Zeng H.
papers.abstract: Background Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a heterogeneous respiratory disease involving airway inflammation, emphysema, and pulmonary vascular remodeling. Manganese exposure has been linked to pulmonary inflammation and oxidative stress, but its molecular association with COPD vascular pathology remains unclear. This study explored a manganese-associated transcriptional signature in COPD and investigated its potential relationship with endothelial cell dysfunction and vascular remodeling. Methods Bulk transcriptomic datasets were used to calculate a manganese-related transcriptional score, identify differentially expressed genes, and characterize WGCNA modules. Manganese-COPD-associated genes were obtained by intersecting manganese-related genes, COPD differentially expressed genes, and manganese-associated module genes. Functional enrichment, PPI analysis, machine-learning-based feature selection, diagnostic modeling, and consensus clustering were performed. Single-cell RNA sequencing data were analyzed to characterize HBEGF expression, endothelial subpopulations, CytoTRACE2 scores, pseudotime dynamics, transcription factor activity, cell-cell communication, and NicheNet ligand-target relationships. Results COPD samples showed significantly higher manganese-related transcriptional scores. A total of 43 manganese-COPD-associated candidate genes were identified and were enriched mainly in pathways related to inflammation, cytokines, immune chemotaxis, and vascular processes. Machine learning identified 14 core diagnostic genes, and the combined model showed good classification performance in the training and validation cohorts. Among these genes, HBEGF showed the highest contribution in the ElasticNet model and was prioritized for downstream analysis. Consensus clustering divided COPD samples into two molecular subtypes with distinct manganese-related scores and functional features. Single-cell analysis suggested that HBEGF was closely associated with endothelial cell alterations, especially venous endothelial cells. Pseudotime and transcription factor analyses suggested a potential JUN/HBEGF regulatory relationship. CellChat and NicheNet analyses further indicated that venous endothelial cell-derived HBEGF may participate in endothelial-smooth muscle cell communication. Conclusion This study identified an elevated manganese-related transcriptional score in COPD and prioritized HBEGF as a key candidate associated with venous endothelial cell state changes and endothelial-smooth muscle communication. These findings suggest a potential JUN/HBEGF-associated endothelial signature relevant to COPD pulmonary vascular remodeling, which warrants further experimental validation.

papers.title: Novel adenoma-immune phenotypes are associated with risk of metachronous polyps and colorectal cancer in a bowel screening cohort.
papers.authors: McSorley ST, Iwata T, Ammar A, Al-Badran SSF, Irvine L, Dietrich CK, Legrini A, de Koning MR, Fisher N, Parsons EC, Dunne P, Sampson C, March GR, Maka N, Jamieson NB, Johnstone M, Lynch G, Edwards J.
papers.abstract: Background Current British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidelines misclassify metachronous lesion risk after polypectomy in approximately 40% of patients. Building on evidence that immune exclusion drives progression of adenomas to colorectal cancer, this study examined immune profiles in screen-detected adenomas as a predictive biomarker for metachronous lesion risk. Methods Patients undergoing polypectomy within the Scottish Bowel Screening Programme, with surveillance colonoscopy between 6 months and 6 years were included (n = 2642). Chromogenic immunohistochemistry (IHC; n = 2466), 6-plex multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF; n = 331), and spatially resolved 6000-plex single cell transcriptomics (n = 7) were applied to adenoma microarrays. Cell density and location were measured using QuPath. Hierarchical then K-means clustering was used to define immune cell density-based clusters, which were compared to future lesion events using Kaplan-Meier curves and the log rank test. Results After adjustment for age, sex, site, size and dysplasia, adenoma CD3 + T cell density was significantly associated with future colorectal neoplasia (OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.20-1.72, p Conclusion Adenoma immune contexture emerges as a possible determinant of future metachronous lesion risk, offering a novel biomarker to refine surveillance.

papers.title: Beyond M1/M2 dichotomy: Toward an operationally defined, modular framework for macrophage functional states.
papers.authors: Jafari A, Vazifedust S, Harmileh KM, Karbasi F, Mazloomi E.
papers.abstract: Macrophages are versatile immune cells involved in tissue homeostasis, host defense, inflammation, and disease progression. Their biology has traditionally been interpreted through the M1/M2 paradigm, but single-cell and spatial profiling, lineage tracing, and multi-omics reveal substantially greater heterogeneity. This review organizes macrophage diversity around recurring functional programs: immunosuppressive/regulatory, matrix-remodeling, hypoxia-associated metabolic, IFN-responsive/antigen-presenting, and proliferative. Angiogenic/perivascular activity is treated as a putative program because its status as a distinct transcriptional entity remains uncertain. We introduce an operational framework based on three criteria-co-expression coherence, combinatorial independence, and microenvironmental inducibility-to distinguish candidate functional modules from broader programs. We also conduct an evidence-weighted assessment of these programs, examining their independent variation, contextual coupling, and co-occurrence. Furthermore, we propose a Macrophage Dominance Index (MDI) as a hypothesis-generating numerical framework, with provisional marker sets, weighting, and formula requiring independent validation. Finally, we derive falsifiable predictions and outline experimental, single-cell, spatial, and clinical strategies to test relationships among programs. Overall, available evidence suggests substantial coupling among macrophage functional programs rather than uniformly independent functional axes. Macrophage heterogeneity is therefore better understood as context-dependent combinations of programs, some of which remain unconfirmed as distinct transcriptional modules. Although the framework may inform macrophage biology broadly, most supporting evidence, particularly concerning program relationships, biomarkers, prognosis, and therapeutic implications, derives from tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). Its applicability to non-cancer settings remains to be established. The MDI and proposed predictions are intended to facilitate testable research, not to serve as validated diagnostic, prognostic, or therapeutic tools.

papers.title: Diet-independent pregravid obesity drives premature but functionally dysregulated fetal immune maturation across multiple immune compartments in rhesus macaques.
papers.authors: Doratt BM, Wagner S, Avila U, Hodge T, Martin LD, Varlamov O, Messaoudi I.
papers.abstract: Pregravid obesity is associated with long-term immune alterations in offspring, but the mechanisms linking maternal metabolic state to fetal immune development remain poorly defined. To address this gap, we used a rhesus macaque model of spontaneous, diet-independent pregravid obesity to examine impact of pregravid obesity on fetal immune maturation and function. We profiled immune cell frequency, function, transcriptional programs, and inferred intercellular communication in umbilical cord blood, fetal spleen, and fetal lung using spectral flow cytometry, multiplex cytokine profiling, functional stimulation assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing. Pregravid obesity was associated with altered fetal organ growth, elevated inflammatory mediators, altered immune cell frequencies, and hyperresponsive splenic leukocyte responses to in vitro stimulation. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses revealed a conserved program of innate immune reprogramming across all three compartments, characterized by heightened inflammatory, migratory, and metabolic signatures together with reduced antigen-presentation potential. We also observed impaired T cell maturation with premature effector differentiation and evidence of B cell dysfunction. Computationally inferred cell-cell communication predicted loss of tolerogenic signaling and enhanced proinflammatory pathways across splenic and lung myeloid cells. Together, these findings indicate that diet-independent pregravid obesity drives premature but functionally dysregulated maturation of fetal circulating and tissue-resident immune cells, providing a candidate mechanism for the increased susceptibility to infection, respiratory disease, and immune dysregulation reported in offspring of mothers with obesity. This connection should be tested directly in postnatal studies.

papers.title: Pancreatic α cells function as MHC class II-dependent antigen-presenting cells in type 1 diabetes.
papers.authors: Li Z, Wu X, Ma S, Zeng Q, Wang X, Xi Q, Jin QW, Jie Z, Wong FS, Li M.
papers.abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease characterized by T cell-mediated destruction of pancreatic β cells, in which antigen presentation is essential. Although professional antigen-presenting cells initiate autoreactive T cell responses, whether endocrine cells contribute to antigen presentation within inflamed islets remains unclear. Here, we show that pancreatic α cells acquire major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II (MHC-II)-dependent antigen-presenting capacity during T1D progression. Reanalysis of single-cell RNA sequencing datasets from nonobese diabetic (NOD) mice and human T1D islets revealed progressive up-regulation of MHC-II associated genes in α cells. Immunostaining validated the increased of MHC-II level both in NOD mice and patients with T1D. Mechanistically, inflammatory cytokines activated the Janus kinase-signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT) pathway in α cells, leading to JAK-STAT-dependent MHC-II induction. Functionally, activated α cells internalized, processed, and presented exogenous antigens, acquired expression of costimulatory molecules, and promoted antigen-specific CD4 + T cell activation. These findings identify pancreatic α cells as nonprofessional antigen-presenting cells and expand the current understanding of antigen presentation in autoimmune diabetes.

papers.title: Integrative analysis reveals shared biomarkers and pathways in osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis using machine learning and single-cell sequencing.
papers.authors: Zhao J, Chen Y, Yang F, Tian C, Luo W, Su Z, Yang B, Liu W, Yang H.
papers.abstract: Background Osteoporosis (OP) and Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) are prevalent chronic diseases characterized by bone loss and immune dysregulation. Evidence suggests that patients with RA are at increased risk of developing OP; however, the shared molecular mechanisms linking these conditions remain incompletely understood. Methods Publicly available bulk transcriptomic and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets for OP and RA were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to identify shared gene modules associated with both diseases. Functional enrichment and protein-protein interaction analyses were performed to characterize common biological pathways. Machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest (RF) and Support Vector Machine (SVM), were used to identify and validate shared hub genes and to construct diagnostic models. Immune cell infiltration was evaluated using CIBERSORT, and the cellular localization of hub genes was further validated using scRNA-seq analysis. Results WGCNA identified 329 genes shared between OP- and RA-associated modules, which were significantly enriched in muscle-related processes, cytokine signaling, and immune-inflammatory pathways. RF analysis identified three shared candidate genes: ANO5, IL27RA, and CNTN3. Among these, ANO5 and IL27RA demonstrated consistent expression evidence and literature support, whereas CNTN3 emerged as a computationally nominated candidate requiring cautious interpretation and experimental validation. An SVM-based model incorporating these genes demonstrated robust predictive accuracy in both OP and RA validation cohorts. Immune infiltration analysis revealed distinct yet coordinated immune landscapes, with hub genes showing significant correlations with T cells, macrophages, B cells, and plasma cells. ScRNA-seq analysis revealed that ANO5 was predominantly expressed in macrophages and fibroblasts, IL27RA was mainly enriched in T cells, whereas CNTN3 showed minimal enrichment at the single-cell level in both OP bone and RA synovial tissues. Conclusion This integrative bioinformatics and machine learning study identifies shared molecular signatures and immune-related mechanisms underlying OP and RA. ANO5 and IL27RA emerge as robust candidate regulators linking immune dysregulation and bone remodeling, whereas CNTN3-although identified by machine learning-requires cautious interpretation and further investigation due to limited supporting evidence. These findings provide novel insights into the pathogenesis of RA-associated OP and highlight potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets for their comorbidity.

papers.title: Effective anti-PD-1 therapy reduces neutrophil infiltration via T cell-macrophage chemokine axis in hepatocellular carcinoma.
papers.authors: Huang J, Yi B, Qi K, Ma D, Sun F, Han B, Zhao Y, Wan W, Zhang N, Liu R.
papers.abstract: Objective Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapies, such as anti-PD-1 treatment, have achieved great success in various cancers, including hepatocellular carcinoma. Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes have major roles in the mechanism of action for ICIs, but numerous other components of the tumor microenvironment also contribute to the effectiveness of immunotherapy. However, little is known about the changes in the tumor microenvironment after ICI therapy, which may sustainably affect tumor progression. Methods Integrated single-cell RNA sequencing data were collected for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patient samples and analyzed to characterize immune cell alterations within the tumor microenvironment. Three different orthotopic allograft HCC models were established for ICI therapy and microenvironment component detection by using flow cytometry and multiple ELISA assays. Transwell assays were combined with flow cytometry to evaluate neutrophil migration. In vitro coculture systems were employed to investigate communication between different cell types. Multiplex immunochemistry analysis was conducted for human clinical samples to confirm the findings. Results Our results indicate that neutrophil infiltration was significantly reduced after effective ICI therapy, but not in patients with failed immunotherapy. Mechanistically, we found that effective anti-PD-1 therapy activates T cells, which secrete interferon-γ and other cytokines that act on tumor-associated macrophages. This T cell-macrophage crosstalk suppresses tumor-associated neutrophil-related chemokines secreted by macrophages. Consequently, neutrophil infiltration into the tumor microenvironment is diminished. Conclusions Our findings show that immunotherapy reinvigorates T cells, but also remodels the myeloid compartment and reduces neutrophil recruitment, potentially alleviating neutrophil-mediated immunosuppression, thereby providing potential myeloid-targeted combinatorial strategies for improving checkpoint blockade responses.

papers.title: Long non-coding RNA RP3-380B8.4 facilitates tumor malignancy, liver metastasis and shapes an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in colorectal cancer.
papers.authors: Zheng Y, Dong L, Lai J, Xie J, Liu H, Huang Q, Cao J.
papers.abstract: Background Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) participate in colorectal cancer (CRC) progression and immune regulation. However, the biological functions of lncRNA RP3-380B8.4 (RP3) in CRC and its relationship with the tumor immune microenvironment remain unclear. Methods RP3 expression in CRC was assessed using public datasets and validated by in situ hybridization (ISH). We further examined the expression levels and intracellular localization of RP3 in CRC cells by qRT-PCR. The effect of RP3 on the cell growth, migration, invasion and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) was investigated by in vitro experiments and western blot. In vivo experiments confirmed that RP3 potentiated tumor growth and liver metastasis in CRC. We predicted the mechanism by RNA-seq, and confirmed them by western blot. The impact of RP3 on the tumor immune microenvironment was analyzed by bioinformatics analysis and flow cytometry. Results RP3 was substantially elevated in CRC tissues and associated with poor prognosis. RP3 overexpression increased CRC cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and EMT in vitro. RP3 overexpression accelerated orthotopic colorectal cancer growth and liver metastasis in nude mice. On the contrary, knockdown of RP3 achieved the opposite effect. Mechanistically, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) and western blot analysis revealed that RP3 overexpression is associated with enrichment of MYC target gene programs and elevated c-Myc protein levels in colorectal cancer. Furthermore, overexpression of RP3 significantly reduced the infiltration of CD8 + T cells in the tumor, while inhibiting the polarization of macrophages toward the CD86-positive (M1-like) phenotype. Conversely, knockdown of RP3 effectively ameliorated this tumor immunosuppressive microenvironment. Conclusions RP3 facilitates CRC proliferation and metastasis and exerts immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment. These findings implicate RP3 as a candidate regulator in CRC whose mechanistic and therapeutic potential requires further validation.

papers.title: Immunoinformatics-based design of a multi-epitope vaccine against Fusobacterium nucleatum-associated colorectal cancer.
papers.authors: Tan CH, Ching JJ, Shuib AS, Sim KS.
papers.abstract: A multi-epitope vaccine candidate, A-20EFγ, was rationally designed against Fusobacterium nucleatum using proteomic and genomic information. The construct comprises a B-cell epitope (epitope 20) derived from the ABC transporter permease, along with cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CTL) and helper T-lymphocyte (HTL) epitopes (epitopes E, F, and γ) selected from the nickel ABC transporter permease. All epitopes demonstrated favorable immunological properties, including high antigenicity, surface accessibility, and the absence of allergenicity and toxicity. These epitopes were assembled using suitable linkers, and outer membrane protein A was incorporated as an adjuvant to enhance immunogenicity. Additionally, the PADRE sequence was included to improve immune stimulation and population coverage, resulting in a remarkable increase in predicted MHC class II and combined population coverage to 99.98%. The three-dimensional structure of the finalized vaccine was modeled using multiple computational approaches and validated through structural quality assessments and molecular dynamics simulations, with the RoseTTAFold model showing superior stability. Molecular docking, network normal mode, and binding free energy analyses revealed stable interactions between the vaccine and Toll-like receptors 2 and 4. Immune simulations further suggested that A-20EFγ could elicit a robust and long-lasting humoral immune response, characterized by high IgG and IgM levels and enhanced memory B-cell activity. Lastly, codon optimization and in silico cloning were conducted to facilitate in vitro synthesis and predict efficient expression in E. coli using the pET-28a (+) vector. Overall, these preliminary findings suggest A-20EFγ as a potential prophylactic vaccine candidate for the prevention of F. nucleatum-associated colorectal cancer.

papers.title: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay-based screening approach for phage-independent affinity maturation of single-domain antibodies.
papers.authors: Wada S, Ito T, Nakazawa H, Umetsu M.
papers.abstract: Because of its high specificity and stability, the single variable domain of the heavy chain of a heavy-chain camel antibody (VHH) is an essential component in diagnostics and therapeutics. However, VHHs derived from immune or synthetic libraries often require affinity maturation to meet clinical or industry requirements. Although phage display has been widely used for this purpose, it is prone to selection bias and requires re-cloning steps. Here, we developed a phage-independent screening system for VHH affinity maturation. We first used single-residue random mutation scanning to identify functional hotspots in the complementarity-determining region 3 of an anti-procalcitonin VHH. Subsequently, we constructed a simultaneous multi-residue mutation library for these hotspots and screened the variants in the library by using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay approach. One of the identified variants exhibited a 70-fold improvement in the dissociation constant compared with the wild type. In addition, we utilized a Bayesian optimization-based machine learning model and explored additional high-affinity variants. Our results demonstrate that this phage-independent approach effectively circumvents the concerns of conventional biopanning and thus provides an efficient platform for antibody engineering.

papers.title: Integrative bioinformatics and preliminary experimental validation suggest the therapeutic potential of lycorine in uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma.
papers.authors: Dong P, Xia L, Zhao L, Liu Y, Gao Z, Han X, Su Z, Ma M, Zhang Y.
papers.abstract: Uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) is one of the most prevalent gynecological malignancies worldwide and remains a significant threat to women's health. Lycorine, a natural alkaloid isolated from plants of the Amaryllidaceae family, has attracted considerable attention owing to its diverse pharmacological activities, particularly its anti-tumor properties. However, the potential therapeutic targets and action mechanism of lycorine in UCEC remain unclear.In this study, an integrated strategy combining bioinformatic analysis and preliminary experimental validation was used to elucidate the anti-tumor mechanisms of lycorine in UCEC. Potential targets of lycorine were predicted using public databases and intersected with differentially expressed genes derived from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) UCEC dataset. Subsequently, a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed, and Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses were used to investigate the biological functions and pathways associated with these targets. Prognostic analysis and Cox regression were used to establish a risk prediction model. Immune infiltration analysis was performed to evaluate the relationship between key genes and the tumor immune microenvironment.Results revealed 10 potential targets of lycorine associated with UCEC. Functional enrichment analysis indicated that these genes were mainly involved in cholinergic synapse and neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction pathways. Three key genes (ACHE, MAN2B1, and PNP) were further identified to construct a prognostic model, which showed moderate predictive performance in survival analysis. Immune infiltration analysis revealed that these genes were associated with multiple immune cell populations in the tumor microenvironment. Molecular docking revealed that the binding energies of ACHE, MAN2B1, and PNP with lycorine were ≤ - 7.0 kcal/mol, indicating stable binding. In vitro experiments confirmed that lycorine significantly inhibited the proliferation of Ishikawa endometrial cancer cells.In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the potential therapeutic effects of lycorine in UCEC and identifies ACHE, MAN2B1, and PNP as promising therapeutic targets for further investigation.
