papers.title: Carbonic anhydrase 4 restrains dual TLR4-NF-κB/IRF3 innate immune signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition in methotrexate-induced pulmonary fibrosis.
papers.authors: Liu Y, Fan R.
papers.abstract: Background Methotrexate (MTX)-induced pulmonary fibrosis (MTX-PF) is the most severe and frequently irreversible manifestation of MTX pulmonary toxicity, yet the molecular target and signaling circuitry linking drug exposure to fibrosis remain undefined, hampering diagnosis and targeted intervention. Methods We integrated network toxicology, an ensemble of 112 machine-learning classifiers and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) with six GEO cohorts to nominate fibrotic-lung genes, which were intersected with predicted MTX targets to prioritize candidates relevant to MTX-PF. Lead candidates were validated by molecular docking, 100-ns molecular dynamics simulation, MM-PBSA binding free energy calculation and surface plasmon resonance (SPR). In vivo MTX-induced mouse models and in vitro BEAS-2B assays, including the Transwell migration/invasion, EdU proliferation, immunofluorescence, RT-qPCR, Western blotting, CA4 and TLR4 overexpression, and a CA4/TLR4 co-overexpression rescue experiment, were performed to assess the regulatory role of the top-ranked gene. Results Carbonic anhydrase 4 (CA4) ranked first by SHAP importance (0.120) and diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.879); the Ridge model discriminated training and validation cohorts (AUC = 0.930, 0.897 and 0.864). MTX bound stably to CA4 in silico (Vina -7.078 kcal/mol; MM-PBSA ΔG bind -76.5 kJ/mol), and SPR detected concentration-dependent binding to recombinant CA4 (K D = 6.25 μM), identifying CA4 as a candidate direct binding partner. In MTX-treated mice, CA4 was downregulated while TLR4, collagen deposition and serum TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, IFN-α and IFN-β were elevated. In BEAS-2B cells, CA4 overexpression suppressed migration, invasion and proliferation, reversed MTX-induced upregulation of TLR4, NF-κB, IRF3, VIM, FN1 and COL1A1, and restored E-cadherin. Forced TLR4 overexpression reversed the protective effect of CA4 and re-established the inflammatory and mesenchymal phenotype. Conclusion In MTX-PF, MTX directly binds CA4 in vitro . CA4 loss accompanies coordinate upregulation of the TLR4-NF-κB/IRF3 axis and an EMT program coupling epithelial injury to fibrogenesis, and CA4 restoration reverses this program in epithelial cells. Although TLR4 gain-of-function abrogated CA4 -mediated suppression, its causal necessity remains untested. Given that TLR4 signaling is context-dependent and can facilitate inflammation resolution in some fibrosis models, therapeutic blockade requires careful attention to cell type and timing. CA4 thus represents a candidate molecular correlate and experimental target, pending clinical and in vivo validation.

figure.caption: The chemical structure of MTX and its potential protein targets. (A) 2D planar chemical structure of MTX; (B) 3D minimum-energy conformation of MTX; (C) the Venn diagram of predicted human protein targets of MTX from three independent databases: ChEMBL, SEA, and SwissTargetPrediction.

papers.title: The pharmacological potential and metabolic risks of Xiaojin Pill in sorafenib-resistant papillary thyroid carcinoma: an integrated network analysis.
papers.authors: Zhang J, Chen J, Su K, Wang Q, Ni C, Chen E, Wang B, Li M, Dong Z, Cai Y, Mei H, Han T, Huang H, Cai Y, Li Q.
papers.abstract: Background Sorafenib resistance limits the efficacy of treatments for advanced papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). The antitumor potential of Xiaojin Pill (XJP) has been demonstrated, yet its mechanisms potentially implicated in sorafenib resistance and combinational toxicological risks remain unclear. This study aimed to examine the molecular mechanisms through which XJP may act on signaling pathways implicated in sorafenib resistance, and to assess its combinational toxicological risks during co-administration with sorafenib. Methods Integrating network pharmacology and toxicology, we identified XJP's active ingredients and hub targets via protein-protein interaction networks. Clinical relevance and immune infiltration were examined in cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), while molecular docking was used to explore the structural affinities. Global toxicity and metabolic drug-drug interactions (DDIs) during XJP-sorafenib co-administration were evaluated with ADMETlab 3.0. Results We identified 43 bioactive ingredients and 78 intersection targets, along with five hub genes ( SRC, STAT3, EGFR, ERBB2 , and ESR1 ) predicted to converge on the PI3K/Akt and MAPK pathways. Clinically, these targets correlated with poor prognosis and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Notably, network toxicology identified a potential herb-drug interaction signal: core XJP components were predicted to bind key metabolic enzymes (CYP3A4/CYP1A2), which warrants examination in dedicated pharmacokinetic studies. Furthermore, computational analysis indicated that combination therapy may act on shared toxicological modules (Ras/Rap1), warranting attention during co-administration. Conclusions In this in silico analysis, XJP was predicted to act on multiple targets converging on PI3K/Akt and MAPK signaling and was associated with immune-related signatures in PTC; these findings provide a basis for further investigation. However, CYP-mediated metabolic interference may represent a potential herb-drug interaction that warrants attention in future pharmacokinetic studies.

figure.caption: Identification of core targets for XJP potentially implicated in sorafenib resistance in PTC. (A) Compound-target network of XJP. A visualization of the interaction network between 43 core bioactive ingredients of XJP and their 150 predicted unique protein targets. (B) Identification of core overlapping genes. The Venn diagram illustrates the intersection of predicted XJP targets, PTC-associated targets, and sorafenib resistance-associated targets. (C) PPI network. A network was established via the Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes/Proteins database to evaluate the functional relationships among the 78 core overlapping genes. papers.title: Longitudinal analysis of the effects of cladribine tablets on B and T cell memory recall responses to vaccine antigens in people with multiple sclerosis.
papers.authors: Csurhes PA, McCombe PA, Greer JM.
papers.abstract: Introduction Cladribine tablets (CladT) are used as an immune reconstitution therapy for multiple sclerosis (MS). Patients are dosed in year 1 (time 0) and again after 12 months. The aim of therapy is to allow development of a reconstituted immune repertoire with reduced pathogenic autoreactivity. However, CladT could also affect the durability of memory T and antibody responses to bacterial and viral pathogens against which people with MS have previously been vaccinated. The objective of this study was to investigate changes in memory recall responses to vaccines over a 2-year period after the initial administration of CladT. Methods Blood was collected prior to the initial administration of CladT and at 5 timepoints (3, 6, 12, 18 and 24 months) after administration from 18 people with MS. The effects of CladT on antigen-specific T cell and/or antibody responses to influenza, varicella zoster, tetanus toxoid, and SARS-CoV-2 were assessed. Results While levels of antibodies remained relatively stable for most vaccine antigens, numbers of T cells specific for the vaccine antigens declined in most individuals, particularly after the second course of treatment. Observations from individuals revaccinated against influenza suggest that revaccination at 18-24 months after starting CladT treatment, after both courses have been given, can restore influenza-specific responses. Discussion CladT treatment can cause a decline in numbers of vaccine-specific memory T cells. Numbers of influenza-specific memory T cells could be restored to pre-treatment levels by revaccination after the second course of treatment. Larger studies are needed to define antigen-specific revaccination schedules more broadly.

The pre-CladT timepoint is represented by the line at 0 in this figure, so symbols below the line at 0 represent a decrease in the number of cells from baseline, and those above the 0 line represent an increase in the numbers of cells/mL blood compared to baseline. Statistical analysis: Friedman test with Dunn’s correction for multiple comparisons. Timepoints significantly different from the pre-CladT value are indicated by the number of asterisks (****P

papers.title: Treg and immune proliferative programs characterize anti-PD-1-responsive endometrial cancer: an integrative single-cell, spatial transcriptomic, and TCGA-UCEC reanalysis.
papers.authors: Zheng Y, Chen J, Wang Q, Li Q.
papers.abstract: Background The responses to programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)-based therapy in advanced endometrial cancer are heterogeneous. The cellular programs associated with such responses remain incompletely defined, particularly when the immune cell composition, spatial expression patterns, and population-level transcriptomic features are considered together. Methods Publicly available TCGA-UCEC and GSE251923 data were reanalyzed using bulk transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and the Visium expression space platform. The GSE251923 dataset included one anti-PD-1 responder and one non-responder; hence, all comparisons between these two cases are descriptive. Prespecified immune- and proliferation-related signatures were evaluated across the datasets, and the Visium clusters were assigned broad marker-based expression compartments. Exploratory quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) assays were used to examine selected transcripts in the Ishikawa and HEC-1A endometrial cancer cell lines under 1% O 2 hypoxia and in primary neutrophils exposed to endometrial-cancer ascites-conditioned medium. These assays were used as ancillary models of condition-associated transcription; neither hypoxia nor ascites exposure was treated as a direct model of clinical immune checkpoint inhibitor response. Results After quality control, we obtained 16,725 single cells that were assigned to 14 populations. Compared with the non-responder sample, the responder sample contained higher proportions of CD8 T cells [+3.1 percentage points (pp)], regulatory T cells (Tregs; +3.3 pp), B cells (+6.7 pp), plasma cells (+5.4 pp), CD4 T cells (+5.9 pp), and proliferating cells (+7.7 pp); the non-responder sample dominantly contained epithelial/tumor and endothelial cells. In TCGA-UCEC (553 tumors and 35 normal tissues), a high Treg signature was associated with longer overall survival [log-rank p = 0.047; hazard ratio (HR) = 0.58; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.34-1.00], whereas a high proliferation signature was associated with shorter overall survival (HR = 1.72; 95% CI: 1.01-2.94; p = 0.046). The responder Visium section showed descriptively higher Treg and proliferation scores with lower epithelial and extracellular matrix scores. Under hypoxia, the two endometrial cancer cell lines showed higher MKI67 , FOXP3 , CXCL13 , PDCD1 , and CTLA4 transcript levels; the ascites-conditioned medium increased PAD4 and ELANE expressions in primary neutrophils. Conclusion The integrated analyses helped identify Treg- and proliferation-related patterns that differed between two anti-PD-1-treated endometrial cancers and were directionally contextualized in TCGA-UCEC. The qRT-PCR assays provide ancillary evidence of condition-associated transcriptional changes but do not validate immune cell states, clinical response mechanisms, or functional neutrophil extracellular trap formation. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in independent treatment-annotated cohorts.

figure.label: FIGURE 1
figure.caption: Exploratory GSE251923 Visium expression space analysis: (A) density distributions of the genes detected per Visium spot in the responder (n = 4,204) and non-responder (n = 3,899) sections; (B) expression space uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) colored by response condition; (C) relative composition of the 18 Leiden clusters in the two sections; (D) CD8A , FOXP3 , MKI67 , and PAX8 expressions in the expression space UMAP; (E) descriptive section-level signature differences calculated as responder-minus-non-responder levels for CD8 T cell, Treg, T cell exhaustion, proliferation, epithelial, and extracellular matrix (ECM) programs; (F) marker bubble matrix for clusters 0–17 using EPCAM , KRT8 , PAX8 , CD68 , C1QA , CD8A , FOXP3 , MKI67 , COL1A1 , PECAM1 , MS4A1 , and MZB1 . The marker patterns support a coarse interpretation of most clusters as epithelial/tumor-like, clusters 0 and 7 as stromal-vascular-rich, cluster 10 as mixed epithelial-stromal/myeloid, cluster 13 as B/plasma-cell-enriched, and cluster 16 as proliferative epithelial-like. These labels represent putative dominant components of the mixed spots and not formal single-cell annotations. Because the GEO data did not contain tissue position files, panels (B) and (D) show expression space projections rather than anatomical tissue coordinates.

papers.title: Spatial and single-cell insights into the prostate cancer microenvironment: overcoming immunotherapy resistance through multidimensional strategies.
papers.authors: Liu D, Tang J, Jiang Y, Zhao J, Shen J, You L, Zheng Y.
papers.abstract: Despite breakthroughs in immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) across various malignancies, prostate cancer (PCa), particularly metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), has shown limited responses to ICIs. This pervasive primary resistance is fundamentally driven by the canonically "immune-cold" and highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) of PCa. Propelled by recent advancements in single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics, this review comprehensively deconstructs the dynamic spatiotemporal evolution of the PCa immune landscape across localized, mCRPC, and lineage-plastic variant stages (e.g., neuroendocrine and double-negative PCa). We systematically delineate how the profound immune-excluded phenotype is sculpted not by isolated events, but by an intricate, multicellular suppressive ecosystem. Specifically, we detail the subclonal heterogeneity, spatial topography, and metabolic crosstalk of key suppressive populations, including specific tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) subsets, regulatory T cells (Tregs), cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). Furthermore, we elucidate the tumor-intrinsic genetic aberrations (e.g., PTEN inactivation, TP53 mutations) and epigenetic rewiring (e.g., EZH2, CHD1, ARID1A dysregulation) that initiate and perpetually orchestrate this suppressive network. Finally, we highlight emerging therapeutic vulnerabilities and future translational directions. Dismantling the microenvironmental barriers in PCa necessitates transcending singular ICI blockade by employing novel combinatorial strategies that target chemotactic recruitment axes (e.g., CXCR2/CXCR4), reverse metabolic plasticity, and abrogate epigenetic silencing. Coupled with high-resolution liquid biopsy biomarkers (e.g., ctDNA, B7-H3+ EVs) for precise patient stratification and cutting-edge synthetic biology interventions, these multidimensional approaches hold profound promise for reversing the dual metabolic and immune suppressive state of PCa, thereby overcoming clinical immunotherapy resistance.

papers.title: SLC5A12 defines an invasive epithelial state associated with immune remodeling and therapeutic vulnerability in HNSCC.
papers.authors: Tang Y, Zhang H, Zhang P, Qu H, Wu D.
papers.abstract: Background Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is characterized by marked epithelial and immune heterogeneity. The malignant epithelial states associated with tumor progression, immune remodeling, and potential therapeutic vulnerability remain incompletely defined. Methods Single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets from three HNSCC cohorts were integrated with TCGA-HNSC and five GEO cohorts. Epithelial-state heterogeneity, inferred trajectories, regulons, cell-cell communication, prognostic features, spatial localization, and ferroptosis-associated transcriptional programs were analyzed. SLC5A12 was prioritized through convergent computational analyses and was subsequently tested by loss-of-function assays and xenograft experiments. CellOracle perturbation, ferroptosis-related drug-sensitivity analyses, and molecular docking were treated as computational predictions. Results Five epithelial states were identified, among which the Invasive population increased with disease progression and exhibited the highest inferred CNV burden. Invasive cells showed enrichment of malignant and extracellular-matrix programs and prominent predicted MIF-CD74/CXCR4 communication with regulatory T cells. Machine-learning, WGCNA, single-cell, and spatial analyses converged on SLC5A12 as an Invasive-state-associated prognostic feature. Computational analyses further indicated a ferroptosis-associated vulnerability profile in the Invasive state and predicted attenuation of invasive and immunoregulatory programs after virtual SLC5A12 loss. Experimentally, SLC5A12 knockdown reduced proliferation, clonogenicity, migration, invasion, and xenograft growth while increasing apoptosis. Structure-based virtual screening nominated ledipasvir (ZINC000150338819) and elbasvir (ZINC000150588351) as top-ranked candidate SLC5A12-binding compounds. Conclusion SLC5A12 is a molecular feature of an Invasive epithelial state associated with HNSCC progression, adverse outcome, and predicted immune-remodeling and therapeutic-vulnerability programs. Experimental loss-of-function data support a tumor-promoting role for SLC5A12, whereas the MIF-Treg communication, ferroptosis vulnerability, CellOracle perturbation, and molecular-docking findings remain computational hypotheses requiring direct validation.
papers.venue: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology

papers.title: Macrophage plasticity in inflammatory and tumor microenvironments: mechanisms, evidence, and therapeutic opportunities.
papers.authors: Zhang J, Wang Z, Wu S, Meng T, Lu M.
papers.abstract: Macrophages are differentiated innate immune cells with niche-responsive plasticity and, in many resident populations, proliferative self-renewal. Single-cell omics, spatial profiling, lineage tracing, and epigenomic studies show that disease-associated macrophages can acquire collagen-producing, lipid-processing, vascular-construction, antigen-presentation, bone-resorptive, or fusion-associated functions. We use lineage-incongruent macrophage state as a descriptive umbrella for phenotypes that deploy a function or regulatory module conventionally associated with another cell type. Six phenomena are compared: functional adaptation, lineage-program borrowing, hybrid identity, intralineage differentiation, cell fusion, and candidate transdifferentiation. We distinguish state plasticity within the myeloid lineage, lineage-ambiguous or hybrid states with co-expression of different lineage programs, and transdifferentiation requiring established cellular origin, source-program attenuation, stable acquisition of a target-lineage network, and target-cell function. Evidence is graded from Level 1 marker observations, through Level 2 single-cell trajectory or spatial support and Level 3 lineage tracing, to Level 4 functional demonstration of the proposed converted identity. Under this framework, TREM2 + lipid-associated macrophages, osteoclasts, multinucleated giant cells, and most angiogenic macrophages represent specialization, intralineage differentiation, or fusion. TAM-to-CAF transitions are the strongest current candidates for cross-lineage conversion, but the evidence remains model- and organ-dependent, and causal human evidence is limited. A PU.1-anchored rewritable enhancer model provides a testable explanation for how macrophages retain a myeloid scaffold while deploying selected modules. Therapeutic proposals are therefore separated into mechanistic hypotheses, preclinical proof of concept, early clinical evidence, and established myeloid-niche therapies. State-selective targeting is promising, but clinical actionability requires validation of target stability, tissue-specific safety, biomarkers, and efficacy in adequately controlled human studies.

papers.title: Gut microbiota-bone marrow axis: how intestinal signals remodel hematopoiesis and immune status.
papers.authors: Chen X, Li X, Song Y, Liu X, Li J.
papers.abstract: The gut microbiota, as a complex ecological system within the host, plays a critical role not only in regulating local intestinal immunity and metabolism but also in influencing hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) function and immune cell lineage differentiation through the gut-bone marrow axis. This review comprehensively examines how the gut microbiota remodels hematopoiesis and immune status via multiple mechanisms, particularly by modulating systemic inflammation, the bone marrow microenvironment, and HSC fate decisions. Special emphasis is placed on the role of Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling pathways in linking the gut microbiota to bone metabolism and immune regulation. The review also integrates recent insights from single-cell sequencing technologies that reveal hematopoietic lineage biases in the bone marrow and explores the development and immune memory of gut-associated B cell populations during early life. By systematically synthesizing recent advances in the interaction between gut microbiota and bone marrow hematopoiesis, this article aims to provide a theoretical foundation for understanding how gut microbiota regulate systemic immune homeostasis and bone metabolism and to identify potential therapeutic targets for future interventions.

papers.title: An eight-gene prognostic signature and its immune associations in gastric cancer: integrated transcriptomic and clinical analyses.
papers.authors: Wen D, Mi L, Zhang Y, Ji Y, Yang B, Yin F.
papers.abstract: Background Gastric cancer (GC) remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) is a major etiological factor in gastric carcinogenesis and has been associated with alterations in the tumor immune microenvironment. However, how H. pylori -related transcriptional features intersect with the broader molecular and immune heterogeneity of established gastric cancer remains incompletely characterized. Methods Single-cell RNA-sequencing data (GSE234129) were used for exploratory comparison according to H. pylori status and to define an initial candidate gene set. An eight-gene prognostic signature was subsequently developed in TCGA-STAD and evaluated in independent gastric cancer cohorts. Model-development optimism was assessed using 1, 000 full-pipeline bootstrap resamples. Immune features were evaluated using CIBERSORT, ESTIMATE, TIDE, and immunophenoscore, while observed anti-PD-1 response was explored in the disease-matched PRJEB25780 cohort. RGS1 was further assessed in an independent immunohistochemical cohort. Results Exploratory single-cell analyses suggested differences in immune-cell composition, T-cell states, and antigen-presentation-related pathways according to H. pylori status. The eight-gene prognostic signature stratified overall survival in the TCGA-STAD cohort and two independent GEO cohorts. After full-pipeline bootstrap correction, model discrimination was modest (corrected C-index = 0.575). In TCGA-STAD, addition of the eight-gene score to a clinicopathological model improved prognostic discrimination. High-risk tumors were characterized by distinct stromal, genomic, and immune features, including higher stromal activity, lower tumor mutational burden, and differences in computational immune-response-related profiles. At the tissue level, RGS1 expression was associated with survival and selected immune-cell features. In the IHC cohort, high RGS1 expression remained independently associated with poorer overall survival (OS) after multivariable adjustment (HR = 2.36, 95% CI 1.36-4.10, p = 0.002) and was accompanied by lower CD8-positive and higher CD163-positive and FOXP3-positive cell densities. In the independent H. pylori -annotated GSE62254 cohort, the five non-ribosomal components showed nominal gene-set-level enrichment in H. pylori -positive tumors (CAMERA P = 0.044). Conclusions This study developed an eight-gene survival-associated prognostic signature and characterized its immune associations in gastric cancer. H. pylori -related findings were exploratory and did not establish H. pylori specificity of the final model. Further prospective validation is required given the modest optimism-corrected performance.

papers.title: Granulomatous lobular mastitis: diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers.
papers.authors: Yang X, Li J, Liang H.
papers.abstract: Granulomatous lobular mastitis (GLM) is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory breast disease of elusive etiology that presents formidable challenges in clinical management. This clinically oriented review synthesizes current evidence on biomarkers according to their potential applications in GLM diagnosis, differential diagnosis, disease-activity assessment, abscess prediction, recurrence surveillance, and treatment guidance. We critically evaluate conventional inflammatory indices, endocrine markers, immune-cell phenotypes, cytokines, complement-related markers, and emerging molecular signatures, while considering the influence of specimen type, disease stage, comparator population, and assay methodology on reported findings. Recent single-cell transcriptomic and metabolomic studies have expanded the biomarker landscape beyond circulating proteins, whereas epitranscriptomic regulation and immune-cell metabolic reprogramming remain emerging areas with limited direct GLM-specific evidence. Overall, routinely available markers such as CRP, ESR, NLR, SII, and prolactin currently offer the greatest clinical accessibility but limited disease specificity, whereas novel immune and molecular biomarkers remain largely exploratory. Future multicenter prospective studies integrating clinical, imaging, and molecular data are needed to develop robust biomarker panels and support precision management of GLM.

papers.title: Nanomaterial-based therapeutic strategies for systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases: from molecular mechanisms to preclinical translation.
papers.authors: Guo H, Xiang W, Zeng L, Xiao W, Sun L.
papers.abstract: Background Systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs) are chronic, heterogeneous disorders in which loss of immune tolerance, persistent inflammation, and tissue-specific injury can culminate in irreversible organ damage and fibrosis. Although glucocorticoids, conventional immunosuppressants, biologics, and targeted small molecules have transformed care, long-term treatment remains constrained by systemic toxicity, incomplete tissue selectivity, variable response, and limited ability to restore immune homeostasis. Main body Nanomedicine provides a modular framework for improving pharmacokinetics, concentrating therapeutics in diseased tissues, enabling controlled release, and co-delivering immunoregulatory cargos. In this Review, we focus on major SARDs-rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and lupus nephritis (LN), systemic sclerosis (SSc), Sjögren's disease (SjD), and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM)-while using selected evidence from adjacent immune-mediated diseases only when it provides transferable engineering or mechanistic lessons. We critically distinguish passive accumulation from demonstrated target engagement, cargo-mediated effects from intrinsic nanomaterial bioactivity, and reduction of collagen deposition from direct mechanistic evidence of antifibrotic action. We also emphasize that acidic pH, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) activity are not universal SARD features but disease-, organ-, stage-, and patient-dependent variables that require quantitative validation before being used as release triggers. Recent single-cell studies further show that macrophage states form disease- and tissue-specific continua rather than a binary M1/M2 system, requiring more precise cellular endpoints. Conclusions Translation of SARD nanotherapeutics will depend less on adding engineering complexity than on demonstrating disease-relevant biodistribution, target engagement, physiologically validated responsiveness, causal mechanism, repeated-dose safety, scalable manufacturing, and regulatory-quality characterization. A disease-adapted, author-proposed framework of complementary evidence domains may support more transparent assessment of preclinical nanoplatforms, without implying a validated linear pathway to clinical use.

papers.title: Mapping the subcellular pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic landscape: a systems-pharmacology framework for predicting combination therapies against intracellular bacterial infections.
papers.authors: Kumar Pinnelli VB, Thangachi SB, Jayashankar CA, Kandi V, Manish GR, Sam KT, Raju Bhupathi Raju PK, Sucharitha AS, Barman A, Sainath G, Singal K.
papers.abstract: Intracellular bacterial pathogens represent one of the most formidable challenges in contemporary medicine. By exploiting host cellular niches, these organisms evade immune surveillance and withstand conventional antibiotic therapies, establishing persistent reservoirs that are difficult to eradicate. Although antibiotic combinations, host-directed interventions, and drug repurposing have shown promise, conventional discovery pipelines rarely capture the dynamic and compartmentalized nature of the intracellular environment. This review proposes a systems pharmacology framework centered on subcellular pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (Sub-PK/PD) profiling to predict and optimize intracellular combination therapies. Mechanistic and translational studies of intracellular drug disposition, host-pathogen metabolism, computational combination design, and biomimetic infection models were synthesized in a targeted narrative review. Particular attention was given to spatially resolved measurements, dual ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing, metabolic flux analysis, machine learning, and organ-on-a-chip platforms. Pathogen-containing vacuoles, phagolysosomes, the host cytosol, lipid-rich macrophages, and tissue lesions impose distinct barriers to drug ionization, accumulation, stability, and target engagement. Persistent infection also produces reciprocal metabolic rewiring: host pathways supply carbon, nitrogen, lipids, metals, and reducing equivalents, while bacterial stress programs alter growth and antibiotic susceptibility. Integrating these processes can reveal shared metabolic bottlenecks suitable for combinations of pathogen-directed and host-directed agents. Computational models can prioritize combinations, but their predictions require validation under physiologically realistic concentration-time profiles. Linking systems biology to localized Sub-PK/PD provides a practical roadmap for designing niche-specific regimens. Such regimens could improve clearance of persistent intracellular reservoirs, reduce ineffective exposure, and limit the emergence of antimicrobial resistance.

papers.title: An experimental-computational framework to characterize immune cell migration in the glioblastoma microenvironment.
papers.authors: Arroyo-Vázquez RB, Mora-Ruiz G, Pérez-Aliacar M, Ranđelović T, Ochoa I, Doblaré M, Sanz-Herrera JA, Ayensa-Jiménez J.
papers.abstract: Background and objective One of the main physiological drivers of glioblastoma progression is the interaction of the immune system with the tumor microenvironment, where secreted chemoattractants establish biochemical gradients that guide immune cell migration and infiltration. Understanding how these signals modulate immune cell motility is essential for characterizing the mechanisms underlying immune activation and suppression. Furthermore, this chemotactic response is significantly moderated by the mechanical properties of the extracellular matrix. Methods This work presents an integrated pipeline combining in vitro microfluidic experiments with agent-based modeling to characterize peripheral blood mononuclear cell migration dynamics under two collagen concentrations: 2 and 4 mg/mL. The pipeline includes a parametric model that is calibrated from experimental data using specific quantities of interest. The calibration procedure itself is first verified against in silico experiments, in which synthetic data are generated with known parameter values that the pipeline is required to recover. Results Results show that higher collagen concentrations are associated with a significant reduction in directed migration. Although this outcome could be attributed to a physical effect, a denser extracellular matrix mechanically restricts cell displacement, the results are more readily compatible with a chemosensory mechanism, in which increased matrix density attenuates chemokine diffusion, thereby impairing the ability of immune cells to orient along chemical gradients. Additionally, a temporal decay in the motility metrics and their associated parameters was observed, reaching statistical significance at the lower collagen concentration, which could reflect progressive immune exhaustion, a phenomenon consistent with previous reports. Conclusions Together, these findings suggest that extracellular matrix density and temporal dynamics modulate immune cell migration in this glioblastoma model. The proposed framework enables a mechanistic interpretation of immune cell migration that complements traditional statistical analysis, providing a versatile platform adaptable to other cell populations and tumor contexts.
papers.venue: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine

papers.title: Magnetic enrichment-coupled flow cytometry for highly sensitive detection of persistent CAR-T cells in spiked and clinical peripheral blood samples.
papers.authors: Abdel Hadi L, Thangamani G, Sheikh S, Hussain SM, Ingel AJ, Ahmed SI, Bencomo Hernandez AA, Al Kaabi FM, Ventura Carmenate Y, Handgretinger R.
papers.abstract: Background Long-term monitoring of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) persistence is essential for assessing therapeutic efficacy, particularly when circulating CAR-T cell levels decline following infusion. Although quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) provides highly sensitive detection of CAR transgenes, it lacks single-cell resolution, phenotypic characterization, and the ability to assess cell viability. Methods In this study, we adapted and validated an automated enrichment-mode on MACSQuant flow cytometry that integrates automated immunomagnetic enrichment with multiparametric flow cytometric analysis to enhance the sensitivity of detecting and quantifying rare CAR-T cell populations. The assay's limit of detection and potential clinical utility were evaluated using CAR-T cell spike-in experiments in peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) backgrounds and clinical blood samples obtained from patients who received CD19-targeted CAR-T cell therapy. Results were compared with a complementary qPCR assay for vector copy number (VCN) detection. Results The enrichment-based workflow enabled same-day detection of viable CAR-T cells by selectively enriching CAR-T cells while excluding non-target peripheral blood leukocytes, thereby substantially improving detection sensitivity at very low cell frequencies in post-infusion patient samples. Concordant CAR-T cell detection was observed between the enrichment-coupled flow cytometry workflow and qPCR. While qPCR served as an orthogonal approach for sensitive transgene detection, the enrichment-based flow cytometry workflow provided additional single-cell information, including viable CAR-T cell frequency and phenotypic characterization. Conclusion By combining enhanced sensitivity with single-cell and functional resolution, this enrichment-coupled flow cytometry workflow complements qPCR-based genomic detection and may serve as a rapid, accurate, and clinically valuable tool for the longitudinal monitoring of CAR-T cell persistence in patients receiving CAR-T cell therapy.

papers.authors: Liu X, Wang Y, Bi Q, Zhang Y, Wang S, Yang P, Pei J, Zhu W, Chen Y, Zhang Z, Chen B, Zhang Q, Zhang Y, Jiang T.
